note: What the Brazil desk's data files don't hold: prices and counts published by others on election night, the historical polls, the three reads, the voting extension, the videos and the sources. Times are as published (ET converted to UTC; Brasília is UTC-3).

marketPoints.label: Flávio leads the count; the market has turned

marketNotes.en: On election day about $30,000 of selling was enough to move Polymarket's Flávio price down 5 points; pushing it up 5 points took about $100,000.
The 11-point drop just after 5 p.m. Brasília time came in 612 trades from about 200 accounts; the largest was about $4,800. No single large order drove it.
The slide began before the TSE paused its count and before the voting extension; no source tied it to a specific event.
By 8:03 p.m. Brasília time, with 25% counted and Flávio ahead by 317,000 votes, Polymarket already had Lula at 79%: traders knew the Northeast and the big cities were counted late.

polls.note: The final week's poll average, turned into a chance of winning with a normal error on the margin. Datafolha's final runoff polls in 2014, 2018 and 2022 missed the margin by 0.3 to 2.2 points; its final first-round poll this year missed by 4.9.

history.note: Seven presidential runoffs since 1989, and the first-round leader won all seven: no candidate who trailed after the first round had ever won the runoff (Metrópoles). The chance shown is (7 + 1) / (7 + 2), a simple base rate with one imagined upset.

markets.note: Polymarket and Kalshi on the morning of the vote (Flávio 79.1% and 79.5%), as the Brazil desk read them.

why.title: More people voted, and more of them voted for Lula
why.en: Abstention fell from 21.08% in the first round to 19.22%: about 2.96 million more voters (TSE). Poder360’s headline the night of the vote: an unprecedented drop in abstention was essential to Lula’s comeback. The day before, Quaest’s Felipe Nunes had said Lula was the candidate most penalized by abstention.

why.title: The likely-voter models leaned the wrong way
why.en: AtlasIntel’s chief executive, Andrei Roman, said Quaest and Datafolha used flawed likely-voter models: rising turnout among Lula’s supporters should have raised their weight, and the institutes did the opposite. He also said his own institute’s longer final field period softened the race’s tightening. These are his claims; the institutes have not published a review.

why.title: After missing Flávio in the first round, the polls overshot
why.en: Datafolha’s final first-round poll had Lula ahead 45 to 42 in valid votes; Flávio won the round 47.0 to 45.2. Three weeks later its final runoff poll had Flávio ahead 51 to 49, and Lula won by 3.6 points. Roman argued the pollsters, under pressure, feared underestimating Flávio again.

why.title: The markets stacked the same bets
why.en: Traders had three reasons to back Flávio, and they all pointed the same way: the polls had him ahead, no first-round runner-up had ever won a runoff, and the polls had just underestimated him. Priced together that came to about 80%, more confident than the polls alone. The markets read the count well: they turned to Lula while Flávio still led it.

why.title: The other candidates’ voters leaned Flávio, but not enough
why.en: Augusto Cury, Renan Santos, Ronaldo Caiado and Romeu Zema took 9.3 million votes in the first round. By The Hinge’s estimate from how the states moved, a little over half of those voters went to Flávio and about a third to Lula: a gain for Flávio of about 2 million votes, smaller than what Lula gained from new voters and from first-round blank and null voters.

facts.en: Lula’s coalition, Brasil Pronto pra Mais, complained to the Supreme Court that Salvador, Feira de Santana and Lauro de Freitas, in Bahia, had not provided enough public transport for voters, as an earlier Supreme Court ruling requires. The complaint reached the court at 4:32 p.m.
Justice Cristiano Zanin extended voting by two hours, to 7 p.m., nationwide, then clarified that it applied only where voting had not yet ended; votes from urns already closed were counted.
The TSE paused its count at 0.25% of sections and resumed at 7 p.m.
The electoral prosecutor’s office opposed the extension; opposition members called for Zanin’s impeachment; ministers of the Supreme Court and the TSE ruled out annulling the election.
No figure has been published for how many votes were cast after 5 p.m. Lula’s margin was about 4.4 million votes.
